sentences.text: Acaenasuchus, meaning "spine crocodile," was a very small, narrow-bodied animal that lived in North America during the Late Triassic.
The animal is characterized by highly developed scutes along its pre-sacral series, where paramedian plates feature thornlike processes running parallel along their posterior sides.
These scutes are highly ornamented with ridges and hollows not found in Desmatosuchus, and unlike that genus, they lack a "tongue in groove" articulation with adjacent plates.

Medial and lateral wing-like structures extend from the ridges of these pre-sacral scutes, while lateral scutes bear two types of horns: conical horns that curve in multiple directions and blunt horns with less curvature.
Its teeth have rounded tips and broad denticles similar to those of R. callenderi, and a large boss forms the dorsal surface of the orbit, possibly representing a fused palpebral bone.
The carapace of Acaenasuchus was highly flexible due to extensive laminae on its plates, enabling swift and agile movement, and unlike Desmatosuchus, it lacked caudal armor and pectoral spikes.

Unlike dinosauriforms, the iliac and ischiadic pedicles in Acaenasuchus are not perforated, and the recovered humerus features three bulb-like structures on the humeral head, though the mid-diaphysis is missing.
Long and Murry noted that Acaenasuchus possessed teeth described as "ornithischian-like" alongside other unique features.
The species name geoffreyi honors Geoffrey Long for his patience while his father was working in the field.

The holotype of Acaenasuchus, a left dorsal paramedian scute, was discovered by Charles Lewis Camp in 1930, and the type species A. geoffreyi was named by Long and Murry in 1995 based on dermal armor from the Blue Mesa Member of the Chinle Formation in Arizona.
Robert A. Long and Philip A. Murry established Acaenasuchus as a distinct genus in 1995.
Besides the holotype, 95 other scutes are likely attributed to Acaenasuchus.

Until 2016, Acaenasuchus was known only from dermal armor, but excavations that year revealed skull, jaw, and backbone bones, including a specimen known as SMU 75403 described in 2020 that includes cranial, vertebral, and appendicular elements along with new variations in the carapace and shield.
Acaenasuchus is considered a terrestrial organism with little evidence suggesting it had semiaquatic capabilities.
Researchers hypothesize that Acaenasuchus occupied a similar ecological niche to smaller archosaurs of the Late Triassic.
Acaenasuchus belongs to the clade Pseudosuchia, which represents the crocodilian line of archosaurs.

Due to lateral osteoderms on its carapace, Acaenasuchus is classified under the broader clade Aetosauroformes rather than strictly within Aetosauria, and Irmis assigned Acaenasuchus to the family Stagonolepididae in 2005.
A 2020 phylogenetic analysis placed Acaenasuchus as closely related to Revueltosaurus and Euscolosuchus.
Acaenasuchus lived approximately 228 to 216.5 million years ago.
Fossil evidence places Acaenasuchus in the Norian stage of the Late Triassic, from 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago.

It is debated whether Acaenasuchus is a juvenile Desmatosuchus or a distinct genus, with researchers citing differences in osteoderm characteristics to argue against synonymy, though Heckert and Lucas argue that the pitting on Acaenasuchus scutes indicates it is a juvenile Desmatosuchus, and some researchers suggest that features distinguishing Acaenasuchus from Desmatosuchus might represent ontogenetic variation rather than distinct species traits.

Despite debates, most paleontologists currently agree that Acaenasuchus is a valid genus separate from Desmatosuchus, and recent studies suggest Acaenasuchus is not an aetosaur but is closely related to non-aetosaurian taxa like Euscolosuchus and Revueltosaurus.
